description: The team consists of members of the Scientific Student Research Club of Biophotonics at the Military University of Technology in Warsaw. It brings together students from various faculties who are eager to expand their interests in fields such as bioengineering, physics, photonics, electronics, and optoelectronics. Example projects conducted in our club include growing plants in regolith-based substrates and developing drones equipped with optoelectronic gas sensors.
summary:
Our project is an offline-capable prototype of a health monitoring application for astronauts. It brings key information into one intuitive dashboard: heart rate and an ECG-style visualization, breathing, temperature, stress, sleep, radiation exposure, and nutrition, including mineral balance and calorie requirements.

An interactive full-body model, created by our team as an original SVG graphic, lets users select body regions to explore relevant measurements. Clear green, yellow, and red indicators highlight normal readings, deviations requiring attention, and potentially serious alerts. A calendar and explanatory guidance make the interface useful even for crew members without medical training.

Our long-term concept connects the application to a sensor-equipped suit worn beneath a spacesuit, enabling continuous monitoring during activities inside a spacecraft and during EVA. The current proof of concept uses simulated data; its thresholds are illustrative and not clinically validated. It is a decision-support tool, not a diagnostic device.

We built the prototype with Python and Flet. AI tools assisted with programming and development of the web interface; the SVG body graphic is our own work. The modular approach can support additional sensors in future missions.
details:
Our project is an interactive health monitoring application designed to help astronauts understand and assess their physical condition during space missions. Its main goal is to present complex physiological information in a clear, accessible way, allowing crew members to recognize potential health problems early without requiring advanced medical knowledge.

We developed a functional proof of concept featuring a centralized dashboard, an interactive human body model, simulated physiological measurements, and a color-coded alert system. The application brings together several health monitoring categories, including cardiovascular activity, respiration, body temperature, stress, sleep, radiation exposure, and nutrition.

One of the main features is our original SVG human body model, created specifically for the project. Users can interact with different body regions to access relevant health information. The interface takes inspiration from video games, using visual indicators to make medical data easier to understand. The design prioritizes readability, intuitive navigation, and quick access to important information over unnecessary visual complexity.

Our monitoring concept is based on a smart, full-body sensor suit that could be worn underneath an astronaut's spacesuit. Sensors distributed across the suit would continuously collect physiological data during both intravehicular and extravehicular activities. Although the current prototype operates on simulated data, its modular design is intended to support integration with real sensors in future development.

The cardiovascular module visualizes heart rate and an ECG-like waveform, while other modules display respiratory parameters, temperature, and additional health indicators. The nutrition module is designed to monitor mineral balance, identify potential deficiencies or excessive intake, and estimate remaining caloric requirements. We also considered visual features such as a body-temperature heat map, stress-related visual effects, and indicators of sleep quality.

An important part of the system is its three-level health status visualization. Green indicates that a parameter is within its configured reference range, yellow signals a deviation requiring attention, and red highlights a potentially serious condition. These warnings can be displayed directly on the corresponding health category and body region, enabling astronauts to identify concerns quickly. The thresholds used in the prototype are demonstrative and would require medical validation before real-world use.

The application also includes a calendar for scheduling health-related activities, an information section explaining medical measurements, and an assistant concept intended to guide astronauts through appropriate responses to abnormal readings. These features aim to increase crew autonomy, particularly during long-duration missions where communication with Earth may be delayed.

We designed the system with major spaceflight health challenges in mind, including cardiovascular deconditioning, muscle loss, disrupted circadian rhythms, psychological stress, nutritional imbalances, and radiation exposure. We also considered the different operational environments astronauts may encounter, such as orbital stations, lunar or Martian surface habitats, and extravehicular activities.

Technology and AI usage: The prototype was developed using Python and the Flet framework, with local simulated data supporting offline operation. AI tools were used to assist with programming, troubleshooting, and developing the application's interface and web presentation. The interactive SVG body graphic is our team's own work, rather than an AI-generated image.

Our project is not intended to replace medical professionals or provide independent diagnoses. Instead, it represents a personal health awareness and decision-support system that could help astronauts recognize changes in their condition and respond earlier.

In the future, we envision integrating real wearable sensors, personalized physiological reference ranges, muscle activity monitoring, and additional diagnostic indicators. Our long-term objective is to create an accessible, modular monitoring platform that supports astronaut safety, health awareness, and independence during extended missions beyond Earth.
